mainTopic: Wrapping up the two views inside רבי יהושע's statement (his tradition vs. his own reasoning), then finding the practical difference between רבי עקיבא and רבי יהושע: whether milk alone shows that an animal already gave birth (חלב פוטר).
overview: This amud first finishes explaining how רבי יהושע's received tradition (לגמריה) differs from his own reasoning (לסבריה) about a goat's discharge. It offers two explanations: whether an animal can give birth before its months are complete (יולדת למקוטעין), or whether part of a day counts as a whole day (מקצת היום ככולו). Next the גמרא asks what practical difference there is between רבי עקיבא and רבי יהושע. רבי חנינא מסורא answers that they disagree about an animal already giving milk: does that milk show it gave birth, so its next offspring is not a בכור (חלב פוטר)? At first רבי יהושע is said to worry about the minority of animals that give milk without giving birth. The גמרא then challenges this from the widow case in יבמות, where רבי יהושע clearly ignores a minority. So it reverses the opinions, backed by a ברייתא: רבי יהושע says milk exempts, and רבי עקיבא says it does not. Finally, a new ברייתא describes a young goat whose daughters and granddaughters reach ten animals for מעשר בהמה. The גמרא questions why the ברייתא needed each goat to have three, and why it did not let the mother give birth again in the same year. The answer to that last question comes on the next amud.

steps.title: Tradition vs. reasoning: can an animal give birth early?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains the gap between רבי יהושע's tradition and his own reasoning. They disagree about whether an animal can give birth after a pregnancy shorter than the full number of months.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to the tradition רבי יהושע received, an animal does not give birth after incomplete months. According to his own reasoning, an animal can give birth after incomplete months.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing an answer it began before this section. It explains why רבי יהושע's tradition and his own logic reach different results: they disagree about early births.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If an animal cannot give birth early, the timeline is fixed. A birth within the first year means the pregnancy began right after the discharge, so the discharge was not a real fetus. If early births are possible, the pregnancy could have started later, so the discharge may have been a real birth and can exempt the next offspring.

keyTerms.meaning: according to his received tradition (what he learned from his teachers)
according to his own reasoning or logic
we say / we assume
gives birth after incomplete (shortened) months of pregnancy

steps.confusionAlert: Both sides here belong to the same person, רבי יהושע. One side is the tradition he received, and the other is his own logic. This is not an argument between two different תנאים.

phrases.english: According to his tradition, we do not say that an animal gives birth after incomplete months,
phrases.notes: 'His tradition' is what רבי יהושע heard from his teachers, as opposed to what he figured out himself.

phrases.english: according to his own reasoning, we say that it does give birth after incomplete months.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues an answer from before this section, which explains the inner contradiction in רבי יהושע's words.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the two statements by an underlying disagreement (whether early births are possible)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי יהושע's tradition and his reasoning seem to contradict each other with no explanation.
steps.terutzMaskana: The tradition holds that animals never give birth early. His reasoning holds that early births are possible, so the discharge may have been a real birth.

steps.title: Another explanation: does part of a day count as a whole day?
steps.stepSummary: A second explanation. Everyone agrees animals do not give birth early. Instead, the tradition and the reasoning disagree about whether part of a day counts as a full day.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or, if you prefer, say that we do not assume early births. Here the disagreement is about whether part of a day counts as a whole day. According to his reasoning, part of a day counts as a whole day. According to his tradition, it does not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a different way to explain the gap between רבי יהושע's tradition and his reasoning, using the rule of מקצת היום ככולו.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now both sides agree there are no early births. The question is only about timing. If part of a day counts as a full day, the pregnancy could fit just inside the first year, so the discharge could have been a real birth. If part of a day does not count, the earliest possible birth falls in the second year.

keyTerms.meaning: and if you wish, say (introduces another answer)
part of a day counts as the whole day
they disagree about

steps.whatToRemember: There are two ways to explain the gap between רבי יהושע's tradition and his reasoning. The first is about early births (יולדת למקוטעין). The second is about whether part of a day counts as a full day (מקצת היום ככולו).

phrases.english: And if you wish, say: we do not say that it gives birth early,
and here they disagree about whether part of the day is like the whole day.
According to his reasoning, we say part of the day is like the whole day;

phrases.aramaic: לִגְמָרֵיהּ — לָא אָמְרִינַן מִקְצָת הַיּוֹם כְּכוּלּוֹ.
phrases.english: according to his tradition, we do not say part of the day is like the whole day.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second, different explanation for the same contradiction answered in step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Alternative explanation based on a different underlying disagreement (how to count days)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: One might think the only way to explain the gap is a disagreement about early births.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even if everyone agrees there are no early births, the gap can come from whether part of a day counts as a whole day.

steps.title: What is the practical difference between רבי עקיבא and רבי יהושע?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes רבי עקיבא, who rejected רבי יהושע's method and ruled simply by what is known. Then it asks what practical difference there is between the two.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי עקיבא said: I did not reach this way of measuring. Rather, whenever it is known (that the animal gave birth, the כהן gets nothing, and so on). What difference is there between רבי עקיבא and רבי יהושע?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes רבי עקיבא's words from the ברייתא. It then asks a question that sets up the next step: how do his rulings differ in practice from רבי יהושע's?
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי עקיבא does not use calculations based on time. If we know the animal gave birth, the next one is not a בכור. If we know it did not, it is. If we are unsure, it is a doubt. The question is: in what real case would this give a different result from רבי יהושע's view?

keyTerms.meaning: I did not arrive at (use) this method of measurement
any case where it is known
what difference is there between (asks for the practical difference)

phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva said:

phrases.aramaic: אֲנִי לֹא בָּאתִי לִידֵי מִדָּה זוֹ,
phrases.english: I did not arrive at this method of measurement,
rather, any case where it is known, etc.
phrases.notes: 'Etc.' points to the rest of his words: if it is known the animal gave birth, the כהן gets nothing; if it is known it did not, its firstborn goes to the כהן; if it is uncertain, it is a doubt.

phrases.aramaic: מַאי אִיכָּא בֵּין רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא לְרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ?
phrases.english: What difference is there between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yehoshua?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי אִיכָּא בֵּין רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא לְרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from explaining רבי יהושע to comparing him with רבי עקיבא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A concrete case where רבי עקיבא and רבי יהושע would rule differently.

steps.title: The difference is whether milk shows the animal already gave birth
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא מסורא answers that they disagree about an animal producing milk. רבי עקיבא follows the majority, so milk exempts. רבי יהושע worries about the minority that gives milk without giving birth.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנינא of Sura said: The difference between them is whether milk exempts. רבי עקיבא holds that milk exempts: follow the majority of animals, and most animals do not give milk unless they have given birth. רבי יהושע holds: there is a minority of animals that give milk even though they have not given birth.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חנינא מסורא answers the question from step 3. The two disagree about an animal that is already giving milk: does that prove it gave birth, so its next offspring is not a בכור?
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי עקיבא relies on the majority (רוב). Most milking animals have given birth, so we treat this one as having given birth, and the next offspring is not a בכור. רבי יהושע does not ignore the minority that gives milk without giving birth, so for him the next offspring stays a doubtful בכור.

keyTerms.meaning: milk exempts (the next offspring from being a בכור)
there is (a difference) between them
follow the majority
a minority
give milk

steps.whatToRemember: The practical difference is an animal that already gives milk: does milk exempt (חלב פוטר)? Hold this first assignment of opinions loosely. Steps 5-6 challenge it, and step 7 reverses it, so in the end רבי יהושע says milk exempts and רבי עקיבא says it does not.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a basic principle: whether we may rely on the majority (רוב) or must worry about a minority (מיעוט) when deciding someone's status.

phrases.english: Rabbi Chanina of Sura said:
Whether milk exempts is the difference between them.
phrases.notes: Picture an animal that came to the owner already giving milk. The question is whether its next offspring is a בכור.

phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva holds: milk exempts,
follow the majority of animals,
and the majority of animals do not give milk
unless they have given birth.
And Rabbi Yehoshua holds:
But there is a minority that give milk
even though they have not given birth.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי חֲנִינָא מִסּוּרָא: חָלָב פּוֹטֵר אִיכָּא בֵּינַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the question of step 3.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: They differ about a milking animal. רבי עקיבא says milk exempts based on the majority (רוב). רבי יהושע worries about the minority, so the next offspring is a doubtful בכור.

steps.title: A משנה where רבי יהושע ignores a possible minority
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא questions whether רבי יהושע really worries about a minority. It quotes a משנה about a widow whose mother-in-law left while pregnant, where רבי יהושע says the widow need not worry.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does רבי יהושע really worry about a minority? We learned in a משנה: if she has a mother-in-law, she need not worry. If the mother-in-law left while pregnant, she must worry. רבי יהושע says: she need not worry.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer from step 4, which said רבי יהושע worries about the minority. It brings a משנה that seems to show the opposite.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 4, רבי יהושע worried about the small group of animals that give milk without giving birth. Here, in a case about a widow, רבי יהושע is lenient even though a brother-in-law might have been born. That looks like he does not worry about small possibilities. The next step spells out why.

keyTerms.meaning: And does he really worry? This opens a challenge.
A minority, the less common possibility
Mother-in-law
Literally 'full', meaning pregnant
She must worry, take the possibility into account

phrases.english: And is Rabbi Yehoshua concerned for a minority?
But didn't we learn in a mishna:
If she had a mother-in-law
phrases.notes: This is a widow with no children. Her mother-in-law went overseas and might have had a son, who would need to do יבום.

phrases.english: she need not be concerned;
if she left full (pregnant),
she must be concerned.
Rabbi Yehoshua says: She need not be concerned.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי חָיֵישׁ רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ לְמִיעוּט? וְהָתְנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of רבי חנינא מסורא in step 4
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 4 that רבי יהושע worries about a minority (milk without birth)
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In the widow case רבי יהושע is lenient despite a possible male birth, which suggests he ignores minorities.

steps.title: Why רבי יהושע treats a male birth as only a minority
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא recalls the reason for רבי יהושע's ruling. Once miscarriages are combined with female births, males are a minority, and we do not worry about a minority.
steps.simpleTranslation: And we said: what is רבי יהושע's reason? He holds that most pregnant women give birth and a minority miscarry. Of those who give birth, half have boys and half have girls. Add the miscarriages to the girls, and the boys become a minority. We do not worry about a minority!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the challenge by showing the reason behind רבי יהושע's ruling. His reason openly says he does not worry about a minority.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Births are split half boys and half girls. Add the miscarriages to the girls' side, and boys end up less than half. רבי יהושע ignores that smaller group. This openly contradicts step 4, where he worried about a minority.

keyTerms.meaning: Pregnant women
Women who miscarry
Combine, attach one group to another
We are not concerned

phrases.english: And we said:
What is the reasoning of Rabbi Yehoshua?
He holds: most pregnant women give birth,
and a minority miscarry,
and of all those who give birth,
half are males and half are females.
Combine the minority who miscarry
with the half that are females,
and the males become a minority,
and we are not concerned for a minority!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the challenge of step 5 by spelling out רבי יהושע's reasoning
steps.raayaObject: That רבי יהושע does not worry about a minority
steps.raayaSupportSource: The known reasoning for רבי יהושע's ruling in the widow משנה

steps.title: Reverse the opinions: רבי יהושע holds milk exempts
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers by swapping the opinions. רבי יהושע says milk exempts and רבי עקיבא says it does not, and a ברייתא says exactly that.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, reverse it. And indeed a ברייתא teaches: milk exempts, says רבי יהושע. רבי עקיבא says: milk does not exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא solves the contradiction by flipping who holds what in the milk argument. It then supports the flip with a ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now רבי יהושע follows the majority: an animal that gives milk has usually given birth, so the next baby is not a בכור. This fits his widow ruling, where he also ignores the minority. רבי עקיבא is now the one who worries about the minority.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, reverse the opinions
Milk exempts the next offspring from being a בכור

steps.whatToRemember: After the reversal, רבי יהושע follows the majority and says milk exempts. רבי עקיבא worries about the minority and says milk does not exempt.
steps.confusionAlert: Step 4 gave the opposite assignment. Do not mix them up. The reversed version here is the final one.

phrases.english: Rather, reverse it,
phrases.notes: Swap the names from step 4: now רבי יהושע follows the majority, and רבי עקיבא worries about the minority.

phrases.english: and indeed it is taught in a baraita:
Milk exempts,
these are the words of Rabbi Yehoshua.
Rabbi Akiva says:
Milk does not exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction raised in steps 5-6
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reversing the attribution of opinions, backed by a ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי יהושע worries about the minority, so milk does not exempt
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי יהושע follows the majority, so milk exempts. This matches his widow ruling.

steps.title: A young goat's family reaches ten for tithing
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that if a young goat had three daughters and each had three daughters, they all enter the pen for מעשר בהמה. רבי שמעון testifies he saw this happen within the goat's first year.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: a young goat gave birth to three daughters, and each daughter gave birth to three. All of them enter the pen to be tithed. רבי שמעון said: I saw one that produced enough offspring to be tithed within its own year.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic with a ברייתא about how quickly goats can multiply, enough to reach the ten animals needed for מעשר בהמה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מעשר בהמה applies when there are at least ten animals born in the same year. Three daughters plus nine granddaughters make twelve. רבי שמעון adds that he saw this happen within one year.

keyTerms.meaning: A young female goat
The pen where animals are counted for tithing
To be tithed (מעשר בהמה)

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
A young goat that gave birth to three daughters,
and all her daughters gave birth to three each,
all of them enter the pen to be tithed.
phrases.notes: Three daughters plus nine granddaughters makes twelve, more than the ten needed for tithing.

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon said:
I saw one that produced enough offspring to be tithed within its own year.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: גְּדִיָּיה שֶׁיָּלְדָה שָׁלֹשׁ בָּנוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new topic after the milk discussion ends
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A goat's daughters and granddaughters can reach the count for מעשר בהמה, even within one year according to רבי שמעון.

steps.title: Why does the ברייתא need three each?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא says each daughter had three. Ten would already be reached if one daughter had three and the other two had two each.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why do I need it to teach three each? Let one of them give birth to three, and the others two each!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the wording of the ברייתא, since fewer births would already reach ten. This sets up an answer that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Three daughters plus 3+2+2 grandchildren already make exactly ten. So why does the ברייתא describe twelve? The גמרא assumes the extra detail must teach something.

keyTerms.meaning: Why do I need it to teach? A question on the wording
Two each

phrases.english: Why do I need it to teach three each?
Let one of them give birth to three,
and the other ones two each!
phrases.notes: Three daughters plus 3+2+2 grandchildren gives exactly ten.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the wording of the ברייתא in step 8
steps.kashyaTarget: The detail 'three each' in the ברייתא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Ten animals are reached with fewer births (3+2+2), so the extra detail seems unnecessary.

steps.title: The ברייתא said three for all of them to keep the wording even
steps.stepSummary: Since at least one daughter must have three to reach ten, the ברייתא said all of them had three.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since there is one daughter that must give birth to three to reach enough animals, the ברייתא taught that all of them gave birth to three each.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 9. It says the ברייתא wrote 'three each' only to keep the wording uniform.
steps.deeperAnalysis: To reach ten you really need one daughter to have three, and the other two can have two each. Since one of them has to have three anyway, the ברייתא simply said all three had three. The extra number is just a matter of how it was phrased; it does not change the law.

keyTerms.meaning: Since; because (introduces 'since it said this, it said that too')
It is not enough; it cannot work

phrases.english: Since there is one
that cannot manage without three,
he taught that all of them gave birth to three each.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַיְּידֵי דְּאִיכָּא חֲדָא דְּלָא סַגִּיא בְּלָא שָׁלֹשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 9 about why the ברייתא said three for each daughter.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Stylistic uniformity: the wording was chosen to keep the cases even
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא's 'three each' seemed to say more than was needed to reach ten.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only one daughter needs three; the ברייתא wrote three for all of them so the wording would be even.

steps.title: Why mention a birth of three at all
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why any goat needs to have three, if each daughter could have two and the mother could give birth again with them.
steps.simpleTranslation: But why do I need to teach three at all? Let all the daughters give birth to two each, and let the mother give birth again together with them!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a new challenge to the ברייתא. It asks why any goat needs to have triplets at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If each of the three daughters had two, that makes nine animals. If the mother then gave birth one more time along with her daughters, that adds one more and makes ten. The question pushes toward the idea that the ברייתא avoided this case because a goat cannot give birth a second time within the same year.

keyTerms.meaning: At all
Two
Let her go back; let her do it again
Together with them

steps.confusionAlert: Count the three daughters and their offspring, not the original mother goat. Three daughters plus two each makes nine, and the mother's second birth makes ten.

phrases.english: But why do I need to teach three at all?
Let all of them give birth to two,
phrases.notes: 'All of them' means the three daughters.

phrases.english: and let her give birth again together with them!
phrases.notes: 'Her' is the original mother goat, who would have one more baby to make ten.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After step 10 explains why it said three for all of them, this asks why a birth of three is needed at all.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's choice of a case where goats give birth to three at once
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Ten could be reached without triplets if each daughter had two and the mother gave birth again, so why describe triplets?
